sections.heading: Owning the truth about my sin
sections.text: Glorious and holy God, I cannot pretend my life has been harmless. I have sinned against you again and again, not by accident only, but with knowledge, stubbornness, and excuses. My conscience has warned me. People who cared about me have spoken truth to me. Other people’s lives have shown me what I should have learned. Even your discipline and your kindness have both called me back. I see now that I have no defense before you.
theological_themes: God is holy, human sin is serious, and conviction can come through conscience, correction, discipline, and kindness.

scripture_references.connection: David’s confession treats sin first as an offense against God, not merely as personal failure or social harm. That grounds the prayer’s honest admission that lifelong sin stands before a holy God.
Paul teaches that God’s kindness is meant to lead people to repentance. This supports the prayer’s recognition that even mercy and patience were God’s summons to return.

sections.heading: Receiving mercy I did not deserve
sections.text: You have seen everything in me, and you would have been right to judge me. Yet you have not treated me as my sins deserved. You have spared me, helped me, and shown me grace. You have not only warned me away from death; you have welcomed me toward life. You have called me to come to you, to receive what you give, and to take my place at your table. Father, I come thankfully. I accept your goodness, and I receive the way you have opened through the gospel.
theological_themes: God justly judges sin, yet graciously spares, helps, welcomes, and calls sinners through the gospel.

scripture_references.connection: This passage holds together human deadness in sin and God’s rich mercy in making people alive with Christ. It directly supports the prayer’s gratitude for undeserved grace instead of deserved judgment.
Jesus identifies the meal with his body and blood given for his people, grounding the image of being welcomed to God’s table in the new covenant rather than vague religious comfort.

sections.heading: Coming to Jesus for everything I need
sections.text: I believe that Jesus, your Son, has more than enough redemption for me. I come to him with empty hands and ask for what only he can give. Teach my mind by his words. Rest my confidence on his sacrifice. Make me glad to live under his authority, not as a burden but as mercy. Let his grace rule me more deeply than my old desires ever did.
theological_themes: Christ’s redemption is sufficient; the believer receives his benefits by faith and submits to his teaching, sacrifice, authority, and reigning grace.

scripture_references.connection: Paul locates redemption and forgiveness in Christ’s blood and the riches of God’s grace. This grounds the prayer’s confidence that Jesus has abundant redemption for sinners.
Paul describes grace as reigning through righteousness to eternal life through Jesus Christ. That directly supports the request that Christ’s grace would rule the believer’s life.

sections.heading: Turning from what put Jesus on the cross
sections.text: Do not let me love the world that rejected and crucified my Lord. Do not let me protect, excuse, or make peace with the sin that brought him grief. When others dishonor him, keep me from joining in, laughing along, or staying silent out of cowardice. Give me a loyal heart—humble, not harsh; courageous, not self-righteous; faithful to Jesus because he first gave himself for me.
theological_themes: The cross creates a break with sinful worldly loyalties and calls for repentance, allegiance to Christ, and faithful witness.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says the cross has crucified the world to him and him to the world. This supports the prayer’s refusal to love the world-system that stands opposed to Christ.

John warns believers not to love the world or its desires because they are passing away and opposed to the Father. This clarifies that the prayer is rejecting sinful worldly allegiance, not despising creation or people.

sections.heading: Learning how to live at the cross
sections.text: At the cross, quiet my accusing conscience with the truth that Jesus has paid for me. But do not let that comfort make me careless. Teach me there to deny myself, to forgive as I have been forgiven, and to submit to you when my will fights yours. Let the cross give me reasons to obey, strength when I am weak, and what I need for the life you have called me to live.
theological_themes: The cross both relieves guilt and trains the believer in self-denial, forgiveness, submission, obedience, and dependence on God’s provision.

scripture_references.connection: Peter connects Christ’s suffering for sins with both substitution and example, calling believers to follow him while trusting the one who judges justly. This supports the prayer’s movement from conscience-cleansing to self-denying obedience.

Paul teaches that saving grace also trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives. This fits the prayer’s request that the cross become a source of obedience, not an excuse for spiritual laziness.

sections.heading: Letting my life match my confession
sections.text: Father, make me real. Let me become what I say I am. If I speak about your truth, let me also do it. If I hear your Word, let me live it. Do not let my faith stay in my mouth only. Make my daily life agree with the gospel I claim to believe. Amen.
theological_themes: True faith should be embodied in obedience, integrity, and a life that matches one’s confession.

scripture_references.connection: James warns against hearing God’s word without doing it. This directly supports the prayer’s closing concern that the believer live what he hears and professes.
John calls believers to love not merely in words but in deed and truth. This supports the prayer’s desire for an embodied, honest faith rather than verbal profession alone.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original phrase about God’s “rod” chastising the speaker reflects a providential reading of painful circumstances as divine discipline. This is biblical in category, but pastorally sensitive because not every hardship should be simplistically interpreted as punishment for a specific sin.

The line about not allowing Christ to be “wounded by others” could be misunderstood as though the risen Christ is vulnerable to fresh injury, or as permission for harsh policing of others. It was rendered as refusing complicity in dishonor to Christ while maintaining humility and love.

The invitation to God’s “table” may allude to the Lord’s Supper, gospel fellowship, or both. The adaptation keeps the concrete table image while connecting it to the gospel and new covenant rather than narrowing it too aggressively.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Gospel appointments” was interpreted as God’s appointed gospel way of coming to him, including the means by which Christ’s benefits are received, rather than as a vague acceptance of religious arrangements.
“Plenteous redemption” was rendered as Christ having “more than enough redemption,” preserving the original’s emphasis on the abundance and sufficiency of Christ’s saving work.
The final contrast between profession, teaching, hearing, and living was expressed as a plea for integrity: that spoken faith, received teaching, and daily obedience would agree.
